zone: Elephant Butte — Sourdough Mountain and Stetattle Ridge
_areas_note: Elephant Butte alone. Confirmed as its own approach and its own permit zone: everything here starts from the Sourdough Mountain trail in Diablo village and runs north-west along Stetattle Ridge, which no other file covers. Deliberately NOT folded into the Northern Pickets file — the butte stands at the eastern end of the Picket chain and a party can reach it on a long traverse from Perfect Pass, but the connector down to Big Beaver is notoriously bad and nobody approaches the peak that way, so Luna Camp and Beaver Pass are the wrong camps for it. Colonial Creek Campground is NOT duplicated from the Ross Lake corridor file; it is a fine place to sleep before the drive into Diablo but it is not on this approach and is already recorded there. The peak has its OWN named cross-country zone, confirmed at six people per party and six parties a night, and the sites below are the two designated camps on the trail plus the dispersed ridge ground the zone actually covers.

sites.name: Sourdough Camp, Sourdough Creek
sites.capacity: A few tent spots only, with a hard limit of FOUR people on the site. That is the smallest party cap of anything on this approach and it rules the camp out for a larger group entirely.
sites.water: Sourdough Creek runs at the camp and is the first water on the whole climb from Diablo — the lower trail has essentially none. Early in the season the crossing can be bridged by snow, which is worth treating with care rather than walking onto.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, collected at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing process. This is a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night rather than open ground, so a walk-up can be refused. A BEAR CANISTER IS REQUIRED here through the main season; the park lends them free at the permit desk. No fires. Pets are not allowed at the camp.
sites.notes: A little over four miles up from Diablo, this is the only designated camp on the lower half of the approach and it exists mainly to break a brutal climb. The Sourdough Mountain trail gains close to five thousand feet in a bit over five miles and is routinely called the hardest maintained trail in the park; the first three and a half miles are relentless forest switchbacks with nothing to drink. Stopping here makes the second day the good one. Note that the climbers' line for Elephant Butte does not continue to the lookout at all — it leaves this trail at an unmarked junction somewhere around four thousand three hundred to four thousand four hundred feet and turns north up the ridge crest west of the creek. No elevation is recorded for the camp because no confident figure was found. Both this camp and the trail it sits on have been closed by fire for most of the last three years; confirm before planning around it.

sites.name: Pierce Mountain Camp
sites.capacity: Small designated camp set among tarns, with the same limit of FOUR people. Assigned by night on the permit.
sites.water: The tarns beside the camp, and they are the only dependable supply on that whole upper stretch. They are shallow standing pools, so treat what you take.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. A bear canister is required here through the main season, as at Sourdough Camp. No fires.
sites.notes: About a mile east of the lookout, on the seldom-used trail that runs out along the ridge toward Ross Lake. Its value to this peak is as the other way in: a party can reach the same ridge system from the Ross Dam trailhead further east on Highway 20, going the long way around Sourdough Mountain, and that is exactly what a recent traverse did when the Sourdough trail was closed by fire. It is brushy and overgrown low down and adds distance, so nobody chooses it while the direct trail is open. The lookout itself is closed to the public and is not somewhere to sleep. No elevation is recorded because the figures found for it were not confirmable.

sites.name: Stetattle Ridge tarn camps
sites.capacity: Dispersed cross-country ground rather than sites. Small grassy pockets and gravel benches recur the length of the ridge, easily enough for the zone's limit of six parties, and no two accounts stop in the same place.
sites.water: Small tarns and snowmelt ponds scattered over the ridge — plentiful in late June, and the single best reason to come early. THEY DO DRY. By August in a warm year parties report water on the ridge becoming a real problem, and which pools survive latest is not documented anywhere reliable. Late in the season carry enough to camp dry.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. There is NO Stetattle Ridge zone — the ridge falls between the Sourdough zone and the Elephant Butte zone, and your permit has to name the one you will actually sleep in. Both allow a party of six and six parties a night. Neither is reservable in advance: they are walk-up zones, issued in person, with a share of the allocation held for same-day and next-day pickup. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow pockets that make the ridge look inviting, and not within a hundred feet of a tarn. NO FIRES in a cross-country zone. Waste in a cathole, or carried out on snow and bare rock. A canister is not formally required in these two zones, but the ridge is open ground with nothing to hang from, so bring one anyway.
sites.notes: This is the camp for the peak. Once the climbers' line breaks out of the trees near six thousand feet the ridge runs north-west in a long open crest of heather, gravel and tarns, and parties simply pick a spot. The best-documented ascent camped beside a late-season tarn at about six and a half thousand feet and went for the summit from there. It is still a long way: from the ridge high point the ground drops something like fifteen hundred feet before you regain that and another thousand to the top, and a full trip is closer to twenty miles and ten thousand feet of gain and loss over two nights. Several strong parties have reached the ridge in a single push and turned round because the butte was still too far. The north-east side of the crest is very steep, so stay on it or just south-west of it. Snow-free is roughly late July into September, which is unhelpfully the same window in which the water disappears.

sites.name: Sourdough Mountain summit ground
sites.capacity: Open ground near the summit, a small party at a time. In winter and spring it is a snow camp with no defined pitch at all.
sites.water: Melted snow in the cold months, which is when this site makes sense. In summer there is nothing at the summit and the tarns further along the ridge are the supply.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Sourdough cross-country zone: six people per party, six parties a night, walk-up only. The lookout building is closed and camping is not permitted at it, so the site is the open ground near the top rather than the structure. Same durable-surface, no-fire and no-meadow rules as the rest of the zone.
sites.notes: The summit sits a little over six thousand feet directly above Diablo Lake, and parties heading out along the ridge in snow conditions have used it as a first night. It is included because the road to Diablo is west of the seasonal highway gate and therefore open all year, which makes this one of the few high camps in the corridor reachable in winter — a late-March overnight on continuous snow is a known way to do the ridge, with the caveat that spring sun softens the slopes badly by mid-morning. For a summer ascent of the butte it is a detour, since the climbers' line leaves the trail well below the lookout and never comes here. It also carries the same warning as everything else in this file: the trail, both designated camps, and the Sourdough and Elephant Butte zones have all been closed by an active fire in the drainage, on top of an earlier fire that shut the trail for two and a half years before it briefly reopened. Check the closure status first; it is the single thing most likely to end this trip.

sites.name: Improvised camp on the shoulder of Elephant Butte
sites.capacity: No established site and no name. Parties travelling the crest report finding flat ground on the shoulder and on the benches near the pass east of the peak, tight enough that three tents felt crowded. Treat it as somewhere you stop, not somewhere you book.
sites.water: Snowmelt and small pools, entirely seasonal. There is no dependable source and nothing to plan on. Fill on the ridge before committing to the descent toward the butte.
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Elephant Butte cross-country zone: six people maximum, six parties a night, walk-up only from Marblemount. Zone camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail and out of sight of both, which up here is automatic. Durable surfaces only, no fires, waste packed out above treeline.
sites.notes: There is no camp at the base of this peak and inventing one would be dishonest — parties sleep where the daylight runs out, on whatever flat ground the shoulder offers. From the ridge the summit itself is not technical, more a broad lump on a crest than a spire, and the standard finish takes its gentle west side at walking-to-scrambling ground. The EAST ridge is a different proposition entirely and has been described by a party crossing it on a long Picket traverse as among the hardest ground of that whole trip, needing roped downclimbs and rappels — so do not read the easy summit as an easy mountain from every side. The named benches near the pass east of the butte belong to the traverse route rather than to this approach, and a party coming from Stetattle Ridge will not pass them. NO ELEVATION IS RECORDED: no account that slept on this shoulder coming from Stetattle Ridge stated one, and the figures published for the traverse-side benches describe different ground.
